title: Farther
html_source:
A striking choice over the more usual ‘further’, suggesting Mulligan has taken on the role of Stephen’s father – a position currently vacant due to Simon Dedalus’s neglect.

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: ‘Further’ and ‘farther’ have different meanings. ‘Farther’ would be the appropriate word in this case, regardless of whether it sounds closer to the word ‘father.’

I’m not aware of two different meanings. I understand that there’s a tendency to use one for physical and the other for non-physical instances in the US, but not in British English, which Joyce uses. Is there another difference that you’re referring to? 

PROPOSED SUGGESTION: There is some dispute over the difference between “further” and “father” both in British and American usage, but there’s never really been any firmly established rule (unsurprisingly). There are conventions, though: American usage does tend towards using “farther” for physical distances, while “further”—to borrow a very questionable construction from the movie Finding Forrester—“is a definition of degree”. It ultimately doesn’t matter, at least for your own use of the words.

See this stirring but still essentially ludicrous movie clip

Also, clogging up these Ulysses annotations with PROPOSED SUGGESTIONS, instead of finding a way to maintain delicately coherent annotations, with suggestions below (which might not necessarily deserve being incorporated even if they are useful and illuminating)—it’s pretty frustrating, and makes sensible judicious edits somewhat difficult, if not impossible.

Still, I think the jarring echo of “father” is very much intended, even if I wouldn’t stretch it to a suggestion of fatherhood for Mulligan over Stephen. Not every association needs to grow into a beautiful butterfly conclusion. Not saying that this tate particularly strained to do that, though; I’m just waffling.
